issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only on the grounds permitted for doing so, and not merely to repair omissions or fill gaps in a party’s case.
material_facts: The party sought, about ten years after filing the appeal, to examine one of the will’s attesting witnesses as additional evidence.
The two attesting witnesses had been identified, but neither had been summoned or examined at trial.
The record did not establish that the witnesses were unavailable despite a diligent effort to obtain their evidence.
The proposed evidence was sought to cure the failure to prove the will at trial.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to admit the additional evidence was not an erroneous or illegal exercise of discretion; the request was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence may be admitted in the specified circumstances, including where the appellate court needs it to pronounce judgment or there is another substantial cause. The provision does not permit evidence to be added merely to fill gaps. The Court relied on The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham (AIR 1965 SC 1008) and Smt. Pramod Kumari Bhatia v. Om Parkash Bhatia (AIR 1980 SC 446), and emphasized caution in admitting belated oral evidence at the appellate stage.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and additional_evidence_sought and attestors_known_at_trial and attestors_not_summoned and evidence_unavailability_not_shown and application_substantially_delayed and evidence_would_fill_gap

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter was an appeal in which a party asked the appellate court to receive further evidence.
predicates.additional_evidence_sought: A party asked to introduce evidence that had not been presented at trial.
predicates.attestors_known_at_trial: The proposed witnesses were identified as witnesses to the document before the trial concluded.
predicates.attestors_not_summoned: The party did not summon the identified witnesses to give evidence at trial.
predicates.evidence_unavailability_not_shown: The party did not establish that the witnesses could not be produced despite a diligent effort.
predicates.application_substantially_delayed: The request to introduce the evidence was made long after the appeal had been filed.
predicates.evidence_would_fill_gap: The proposed evidence was intended to make up for a failure to prove an essential part of the party’s case at trial.

issues.definition: In an appeal, when a delayed request concerns known witnesses who were not summoned, their unavailability was not shown, and the evidence would fill a gap, the additional-evidence request is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A will requiring attestation is not duly proved by the evidence of its scribe alone when the named attesting witnesses are not examined and the scribe signed only as its writer, without an established intention to attest.
material_facts: The dispute required proof of a will relied on to support a claim to property.
The will named two attesting witnesses, but neither was examined, and no attempt was made to summon either one.
The party did not establish that the attesting witnesses were unavailable after an honest and diligent search.
The scribe testified that he wrote the will and signed it as the writer; the will also described him as its writer.
Although the scribe testified about the execution, the document did not establish that he subscribed his signature with an intention to attest as a witness.
issues.conclusion: The scribe’s signature and evidence did not satisfy the statutory requirement of attestation or proof of the will; the will was not duly proved and could not have the claimed legal effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act requires a will to be attested by two or more witnesses in the prescribed manner. Section 68 of the Evidence Act requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act defines attestation and requires a witness to sign with animo attestandi, or an intention to attest. A scribe’s signature for the purpose of writing or identifying the document is not, without the required intention, an attesting signature. The Court relied on M.L. Abdul Jabhar Sahib v. H.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons (1969 (3) SCR 513), Girja Datt v. Gangotri Datt (AIR 1955 SC 346), and H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma (1959 Supp. (1) SCR 426).

rule.if: will_reliance_case and will_requires_attestation and named_attestors_not_examined and named_attestors_not_summoned and their_unavailability_not_shown and scribe_signed_as_writer and scribe_intent_to_attest_not_shown

predicates.will_reliance_case: A party relied on a will to establish a legal claim.
predicates.will_requires_attestation: The document relied on was a will that had to be witnessed by attestors.
predicates.named_attestors_not_examined: The persons identified as attesting witnesses did not give evidence in court.
predicates.named_attestors_not_summoned: The party did not ask the court to summon the identified attesting witnesses.
predicates.their_unavailability_not_shown: The party did not establish that the identified witnesses could not be found after an honest and diligent search.
predicates.scribe_signed_as_writer: The person who wrote the document signed it in the capacity of its writer.
predicates.scribe_intent_to_attest_not_shown: The evidence did not establish that the writer signed to bear witness to the execution of the document.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a will requiring attestation, the named attestors are not examined or summoned, their unavailability is not shown, and the scribe signed as a writer without an established intention to attest, the will is not duly proved.
